question: The Financial Times has recently reported on the EU’s plan to pay out up to EUR 164.5 million under an agreement concluded in 2023. The funds are designed to help Tunisian forces manage migration policy, in an attempt to cut the number of migrants arriving in Europe. The figure is much higher than the funds initially earmarked for that purpose and the human rights situation in Tunisia raises even more concerns.

There are worries that the funds could potentially strengthen the Saied regime, leaving more migrants to have their human rights violated in the most vile manner. Given that more than EUR 6 million have been spent on agreements of this kind over the last six years: 1.
How does the Commission reconcile this situation with the EU’s human rights commitments?
How is the use of those funds being monitored and what conclusions can be drawn?
What issues have arisen in countries with these kinds of agreement, and what measures have been adopted to ensure human rights are fully upheld by the authorities?
answer: As part of the memorandum of understanding with Tunisia (MoU) (1), the Commission has allocated EUR 105 million on migration-related funding in 2023 covering border management, anti-smuggling and anti-trafficking, protection and return and reintegration. Over half of the amount has already been contracted.

The 2023 allocation has to be seen in the light of a comprehensive approach to migration covering all priorities, including on legal migration. As part of the implementation of the MoU, the Commission advocates for the Tunisian authorities to improve their protection policies, for example, by providing shelter and basic services to migrants, asylum seekers and vulnerable people.
EU funded border management and anti-smuggling programmes in Tunisia ensure that human rights principles are respected, integrating human right standards in all programme components.

For example, one element of EU support concerns establishing a specific training academy for which modules on human rights, rule of law principles and international standards will be included in the training curriculum in order to ensure its sustainability. On the monitoring, all contracts have human rights clauses that allow the EU to adjust funding as necessary.

The Commission monitors its programmes through several means, including regular reports from implementing partners and the EU Delegation in Tunisia, external evaluation, verification missions and results-oriented monitoring exercises.

In addition, the Commission will set up in 2024 an independent monitoring system for migration-related programmes implemented in Tunisia, as an oversight mechanism to gain regular feedbacks on contracts, including on do-no-harm and human rights compliance. Respect for human rights and democratic principles is the basis of the EU’s partnerships with all partner countries, including Tunisia.
Commission services, together with the European External Action Service, follow closely the human rights situation and have taken it up with the Tunisian authorities at all levels.
